newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: New Moldovan leader seen backing market reforms.
newsitem.headline: New Moldovan leader seen backing market reforms.

text.p: Petru Lucinschi, elected Moldovan president last week on a centre-left platform calling for social welfare and an end to "savage capitalism", has called for international help in introducing "radical" market reforms.

Foreign observers, and notably the International Monetary Fund which is Moldova's biggest Western creditor, say they are confident Lucinschi will now press ahead with reforms that were held up by feuding between his predecessor Mircea Snegur and the outgoing government.
The 56-year-old chairman of parliament, who was once a secretary of the Soviet Communist party's Central Committee, beat Snegur in a December 1 election run-off.
During a bitter campaign, he criticised Snegur's calls for drastic market reform and said the poor needed more protection.
Snegur accused Lucinschi of planning to restore communism.

Since his election, Lucinschi, who now presents himself as a moderate social democrat, has sought good relations with poverty-stricken Moldova's international creditors as he goes about forming a government. He will take office on January 15.

On Monday, state radio quoted the president-elect telling U.S. officials: "Moldova will continue economic reforms. But in contrast to the previous period, we would like to achieve this task by radical means. In this respect, we are hoping for the support of the United States and, in particular, of USAID."
USAID is Washington's foreign aid agency.

The IMF's resident representative in Chisinau, Mark Horton, told Reuters this week: "My impression is that Mr Lucinschi is a committed reformer...We expect a great deal from him and his government in the way of reforms."
Political analyst Oazu Nantoi said Snegur's reforms were limited: "The pace of reform slowed long before the election."
Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, who was knocked out in the first round of the election and backed Lucinschi in the run-off, resigned last week with his government.

Lucinschi, who plans to use his contacts in Moscow to secure the Russian fuel supplies that the cash- and energy-starved country needs and to reconcile the breakaway Russian-speaking Dnestr region, says he will form a coalition government of "national trust".

He says it could include both his allies -- social democrats and communists -- and Snegur supporters. Right-wing pro-Romanian nationalists have promised to fight what they call Lucinschi's "neocommunism" at parliamentary elections due in early 1998.
Local media speculate Sangheli's deputy prime ministers, Ion Gutu and Valeriu Bulgari, are top candidates for prime minister, along with National Bank chairman Leonid Talmaci.
Horton said the IMF expected Lucinschi to speed up structural reform and improve financial discipline -- the two major issues put off by Sangheli in the run-up to the election.
He said the IMF saw Lucinschi as helping promote the unfettered buying and selling of Moldova's agricultural land, which parliament delayed for further legislation when Snegur proposed it.
Among the president-elect's other policies, the IMF expects privatisation of the energy sector, improving the energy tariff system, fighting tax evasion and applying the bankruptcy law.
Moldova has achieved relative financial stability since winning independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. It has been backed by IMF loans worth some $250 million.
But gross domestic product is expected to shrink again this year, by some two percent, leaving the mainly rural nation of 4.3 million among the poorest in Europe.
Lucinschi sees Moldova's economy "as a market but socially orieNTED" AND with "more rigorous state controls". The IMF acknowledges that in some areas more state control could help.

"There is a need to step up enforcement by the state of the bankruptcy law, to prevent settlements in barter, to improve customs controls, to make big companies pay their taxes...so that even a man on the street understands that the government is serious about enforcing financial discipline," Horton said.
